Chapter 08

Stored patterns and presets

The DTO — the pattern as JSON without a Note in it — and three presets written as strings you can read like a drum machine.

By the end of this chapter

Keep one boundary between the model and its storage form, and see how a small string notation makes test data and seeds readable.

The database keeps a pattern as one JSON column, and JSON has no idea what a Note is. The DTO is the conversion in both directions, with a schema for what comes *out* of the column — because a row written by last year’s version of the app is exactly as untrusted as a request body.

Only two places touch a DTO: the storage layer, and the publish form, which carries the pattern in one hidden field because a form field cannot hold a class either. Everything else in the project works with Pattern. Keeping that boundary narrow is what lets the Note class exist at all.

Three grooves as strings

Why strings and not arrays of objects

A groove is something you *read*. x---x---x---x--- is four on the floor to anybody who has seen a drum machine; sixteen { velocity: 112 } objects are not. The notation costs two small parsing functions and buys presets, seeds and test fixtures that a person can check by eye — which is how the boom-bap hi-hat pattern was noticed to be wrong the first time.

Checkpoint

  • You can say which two places in the project use a DTO and why nothing else does.
  • You can write a new four-track preset in the string notation without looking at the parser.
